newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Sliding prices hit Australia commodities.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Sliding prices hit Australia commodities.

text.p: Sliding prices have dampened Australia's commodity export prospects in 1996/97 to June 30 but the value of the country's mineral and agricultural exports will still be up on the previous year at A$59.7 billion (US$47.16 billion), the government's commodity forecaster said on Tuesday.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) forecast that the total value of Australian commodity exports will rise 4.3 percent in the current financial year.
This is down from ABARE's June forecast of A$61.1 billion and is the agency's second downgrading of Australia's export growth prospects in successive quarters.
In June ABARE lowered its forecast from the A$62.6 billion predicted in March.
Commodity exports represent about three-quarters of all Australian merchandise export revenue.
One of the main culprits behind the latest reduced forecast is falling world wheat prices.

Australia is headed for a bumper wheat crop of about 20 million tonnes in 1996/97, the second highest on record. But big crops also being produced in the U.S., Canada, Argentina and China have sent world wheat prices into a disappointing decline.

"World and Australian grains prices are forecast to fall in 1996/97 as the tight supply situation of 1995/96 eases with a recovery in world grains production," ABARE said in its September quarter outlook publication.
ABARE also said wool prices would remain flat in 1996/97, as stocks in Australia smothered the effect of rising demand.

Australian wheat exports are expected to return A$3.0 billion in 1996/97, down from A$3.4 billion the year before, while wool is forecast to bring in a relatively steady A$3.8 billion against A$3.6 billion in 1995/96.
Added to this, beef export returns are forecast to remain low at A$2.2 billion, down from A$2.4 billion the year before.

Even sugar, headed for a record crop of 5.5 million tonnes in 1996/97, is forecast to bring in reduced export returns of A$1.4 billion against A$1.6 billion the year before. Minerals present a brighter picture.

While ABARE forecasts the total value of Australian rural exports will be virtually steady on A$22.8 billion in 1996/97, against A$22.7 billion the year before, the value of minerals exports are forecast to rise to a new record of A$37.0 billion from A$34.5 billion in 1995/96.
Prices for the majority of metals have tended to drift lower, ABARE said in its latest forecast.
Gold prices are forecast to rise just 2.1 percent on 1995 leaving the value of Australian exports of the precious metal in 1997 at A$5.4 billion against A$5.6 billion the year before.
Exports of uranium (A$310 million), crude oil (A$2.1 billion) and natural gas (A$2.0 billion) are also forecast to contribute substantially.

But lead, zinc, copper, titanium, zircon, iron ore, alumina and steel are all returning increased export values, contributing to a forecast 4.2 percent rise to A$22.7 billion in metals and minerals exports in 1996/97.
Energy is Australia's main export star, with total export earnings forecast to rise by 12 percent to A$14.3 billion in 1996/97.
Coal is forecast to contribute most, with expected export earnings said to rise by six percent to A$8.2 billion.
